### Is the commodity boom over for copper? 



- As 2012 draws to a close there remains one, persistent, unanswered, industry question.  Is the commodity boom over for copper? 



- This paper will answer if the commodity boom is over for the copper market.  To analyse the future performance of the copper industry this paper will focus on future physical growth prospects for the copper market, future price expectations and future profit expectations.

### Is the commodity boom over for Copper? 

As 2012 draws to a close, there remains one, persistent, unanswered, industry question.  Is the commodity boom over for copper?  As the chart below shows, there have been many comments on the commodity boom and the fate of the copper market.  Until recently most were decidedly gloomy. 

#### Do people believe the commodity boom is over? 

Whether they are right or wrong there has been an impact on sentiment 



- Commodities: Supercycle jitters slow projects (Jack Farchy, FT Oct-12) 

- The global boom in commodity prices is over (Martin Ferguson, Australian Resource Minister, Sep-12) 

- Mining boom over in two years (Deloitte Access Economics, Jul-12) 

- Sun to set on commodities supercycle (Morgan Stanley, May-12)

- Commodity ‘Super Cycle’ may be coming to end (Citigroup, Apr-12) 

This paper will answer if the commodity boom is over for the copper market.  To analyse the future performance of the copper industry this paper will focus on future physical growth prospects for the copper market, future price expectations and future profit expectations.  Positive profit expectations, in particular, are a pre-requisite of any prolonged commodity boom.  Volume growth and price growth without profit is not a boom scenario.  This paper will also analyse the industry on a segmented basis. Segments will include; low cost copper miners, high cost copper miners, mineral extraction support services, copper smelters & refineries, the semis industry and investors in copper. 

### 2012 in a nutshell 

Statistics for 2012 suggest a slowdown in the copper commodity boom has already started.  Global refined copper consumption growth has slowed this year in both absolute and percentage terms to 360,000t and 1.9% respectively.  LME 3-month copper prices will average approximately $7,950/t in 2012, a year-on-year fall of 10%.  CRU believes there has also been a slowdown in investor activity resulting in a reduction in investor influence on copper prices. 

Copper mine operating costs have remained stable in 2012 with CRU’s Value Based Costing (VBC) global weighted site cost curve relatively unchanged year-on-year.  Finally, the size of the copper pie, using a simple calculation of refined copper consumption * LME 3 month price, will have fallen by 8% in 2012 to $156bn.  These crude indicators certainly suggest the sustainability of the copper boom should be examined.

### Prospects for copper consumption – the fundamental foundation of a boom 

According to updated numbers from the Copper Market Outlook October 2012, CRU is optimistic that refined copper consumption growth will accelerate during the period 2012 – 2017, registering significantly higher CAGR growth over this five year period than the previous five years.  CRU expects refined metal growth in 2012 of 360,000t (+1.9%).  This growth is forecast to come from China (+386,000t), the rest of Asia (+54,000t) and North America (+75,000t).  Europe is forecast to show the largest contraction (-169,000t) and other regions are largely unchanged.  Looking forward CRU expects refined consumption will grow by an average of over 4% per annum from 2012 to reach 24.4Mt by 2017. 

The US market will contract in 2013 due to the commissioning of the new copper scrap consuming wirerod mill jointly owned by Steel Dynamics and La Farga.  Production from this mill will directly displace refined copper consumption in the region.  Beyond 2013 and through to 2017 growth will be good.  Driven by a continued strong auto sector and a rebound in the construction sector, growth will exceed 3% each year and total 1.8Mt by 2017.

CRU does not expect the refined copper market in Western Europe to reach the bottom before mid-2013. German refined copper consumption will be the first major European market to stage a recovery (given its automotive and manufactured products export market exposure), rising by 1.7% to achieve an annual refined copper demand level of 1.1Mt.  Beyond 2013, CRU’s base case assumes economic recovery in Europe - even under this scenario total refined copper growth from 2012-2017 is limited to 383,000t. Europe is just not as important as it used to be for the global copper market. 

Chinese refined consumption should pick up in 2013 H1 as the impact of the recent stimulus measures comes through, scrap supplies remain constrained by lower availability outside the country, and as the economies of many of China’s more troubled export markets begin to see a recovery.  CRU forecasts a growth rate of over 6% in 2013, up from this year’s figure of 5%.  In 2014, we expect to see refined consumption growth peak at over 7%, before a long term slow deceleration kicks in, reaching a rate of 5.4% in 2017, which equates to consumption of just over 11Mt.  An additional 1Mt of consumption growth through to 2017 will come from other important economies such as India, South Korea and Turkey. 

If refined global copper consumption grows in line with expectations, consumption will have easily fulfilled its part to extend the copper commodity boom.  In comparison to the average of 1.8% per annum growth delivered from 2007 to 2012, refined copper consumption prospects look relatively healthy. 

### How have miners performed in the commodity boom? 

All operating copper mines have benefitted from higher copper prices this and the last decade.  While revenues and profits have multiplied since the beginning of the century, there has also been significant challenges to the sector.  Three of the biggest are shown below:

1. Equipment shortages have made it difficult for mine expansions and mine development to take place to schedule.  The late commissioning of projects has exacerbated market deficits, driving prices even higher.  The unprecedented equipment demand also accelerated equipment prices, itself adding to mine costs inflation. 

2. Mine cost inflation has also been impacted by other shortages and factors such as labour costs and raw materials inflation in areas such as steel. 

3. Political intervention has also been troublesome for the sector.  Governments and other stakeholders have witnessed the improvement in market prices and profits and demanded a greater share of the revenues.  The copper industry has not helped its own cause by promoting a cost methodology that excludes sustaining and working capital costs.  But as the chart below demonstrates, this has created a lower ‘published cost’ that implies a higher ‘operating profit’ and suggests a l

However, the benefits for miners over this period have easily outweighed these challenges. Benefits have included: 1. The construction of new Chinese copper smelters in excess of concentrate production growth leading to intense competition for mined ores. 2. An insatiable Chinese physical demand for copper supporting stronger copper prices as market deficits occurred. 3. This insatiable Chinese demand also encouraged investment funds into the commodity sector creating a large positive investor influence on the copper price. 4. Strong cash flows and strong projected cash flows, used initially to pay down Global Financial Crisis (GFC) debt, and then as a basis to fund further expansions, acquisitions and developments. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 4 of 13 December 2012 Copper Studies www.crugroup.com ### What are miners worried about in the future? Looking beyond 2012, copper miners express many concerns for the future. Our Santiago-based copper analysts offer the following list of worries for South American miners today, which also largely reflect global worries. The meta-themes of raw material availability, cost inflation and political concerns remain unchanged: - In Chile, there are concerns about the availability of qualified labour in the future. Some companies have said that they have plans to internalise part of their workforce (after a long period of externalisation and increase in the share of contract workers) to retain them. There is anecdotal evidence that medium sized companies are having trouble keeping their workers, as salaries and conditions are better at the bigger mines and projects. - Energy and water availability is another important concern in Chile, especially after the rejection of the Castilla power generation plant by the Chilean Supreme court. Many other power projects have been rejected or delayed. The cost of water desalination and especially of water transport is related to the availability and price of energy. Both are expected to increase. - Some concerns have recently arisen about the competitiveness of the Chilean copper industry. As ore grades become lower, operating costs increase and capital expenditure continues to grow. - Miners have cited a slowdown of mine project development in Peru and power development in Chile due to community resistance. It may

just be a matter of time before mine development is affected in Chile in the same way. - Wider community relationship challenges exist over the expected contribution of mining to local economies, as well as compensation for the use of common resources. Next year the ILO169 regulations should be in place according to the Chilean government, and a clearer picture will emerge as to what exactly will be required of projects. The reasons for conflict vary from place to place but can include: - negotiations of royalties or other forms of contribution with local governments or communities. - use of common resources, especially water (or glaciers) that are important for agriculture further down the river system. - air quality, as in Calama in northern Chile, which was recently declared a “saturated” zone, due to the amount of dust. - placement of tailing dumps, sometimes close to communities, which leads to opposition. ### What is the outlook for copper miners? Despite all of the concerns, CRU’s analysis shows that the commodity boom is not yet over for low cost copper miners. The copper operating profit chart on p.6 illustrates this point. copper mines in Chile. This shows that margins peaked in 2011 at over $6,000/t for these low cost mines. The chart also shows that margins have declined in 2012 and that CRU predicts they will decline further from 2015. This shows that the copper boom is not over for existing low cost miners who have another 24 months of strong margins to come. Even beyond 2015, margins for this class of asset will remain substantially higher than historical long term averages. However, CRU believes that the commodity boom is over for high cost copper miners. High cost miners and developers face a multitude of threats. Five key threats to an existing high cost copper miner or high cost mine developer are shown in the chart overleaf: 1. As the chart above shows, CRU expects LME copper prices to decline from 2013–2017. As a result, CRU expects to see marginal copper mines and project costs begin to intersect with copper prices at the end of this period. In addition, smaller

developers, already facing a difficult financing market, will see expected cashflows from the first 12 months of their operations reduce. This is likely to slow down the development of these mines. 2. With persistent refined metal surpluses predicted until beyond 2017, it is no longer possible to assume all additional copper mine supply will be required by the market. Demand growth, although good, is insufficient to soak up all expected mine supply. 3. New low cost copper mine production will continue to commission, particularly during the next 2436 months. 15 projects have been commissioned in 2012 with a further 19 due to commence operations in Q4 2012. Consequently, mine production is expected to grow by over 2.6Mt from 2012-2015. By comparison, mine production only grew by 563,000t from 2009-2012. 4. High cost producers may find themselves competing with more ‘flexible’ high cost production. There may be political, geographic, local economic or by-product revenue reasons why mines in the fourth quartile continue to operate, despite your cost curve telling you they should not. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 6 of 13 Copper Studies December 2012 www.crugroup.com 5. Finally, the threat of cost escalation will persist even though cost pressures may ease in the very short term. The commodity boom is probably over for high cost miners

An important issue to note is that CRU forecasts that Chinese domestic mine production is now reaching a plateau, having increased by 50% since 2009 to reach over 1.6Mt by 2012. This means Chinese mining companies are increasingly likely to raise their production holdings through overseas acquisitions. The author expects to see more bids for copper companies, such as the ongoing takeover bid by Cathay Fortune Investment Limited for Discovery Metals Limited, owners of the Boseto Copper Project. It also expects to see further disposals of noncore assets to Chinese investors, such as Rio Tinto’s binding agreement to sell its 57.7 per cent effective interest in Palabora Mining Company Limited to a consortium comprising South African and Chinese entities. Anglo American also sold its stake in Palabora. One strategy for high cost miners and developers, facing uncertain times, will be to cash-out or exit the market. However, sellers will need to recognise they are now in a market with a weaker outlook, less buyers and more difficult funding conditions than 12 months ago. ### Innovate to flourish in the mineral extraction support ### sector Next, we

move on to the Mineral Extraction Support Sector, those who support the mining sector. We believe that innovative support services will continue to flourish. We can consider one small sector – mine truck tyres – as an example of a flourishing sector. Clearly the sector has benefitted from the growth in ore volumes. However, like many sectors, it was caught out by unexpected demand leading to shortages and to all sorts of stop gap measures. As the chart on p.8 shows, the industry has reacted and there have been traditional and innovative solutions as a result of the truck tyre shortages. Some, such as those on the left of the chart, reacted by increasing production capacity for mining tyres. These tended to be established Western tyre companies. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 7 of 13 Copper Studies December 2012 www.crugroup.com Others, in the centre, were attracted to the market or sought local partnerships to increase market share. These companies focussed on Asian market development and tend to be Chinese start-up companies or Japanese companies looking to work with Chinese partners. Capacity expansions, new market entrants and new market partnerships can all be viewed as traditional responses to a market supply shortage. Innovative support services will continue to flourish
Resulting in investment, increased competition and innovation
The most interesting development and most likely to have a profound impact on the future of the copper commodity boom has been the emergence of innovators, highlighted to the right in the chart above. Taking an entirely different approach, the companies recognised that tyres themselves have become valuable commodities and therefore they set about increasing the life or securing supply of this commodity. A whole new industry had been formed. TyreSense and TMS developed new monitor systems to optimise tyre pressures and increase tyre lifespan. RUD have developed a variety of tyre sidewall chain and chain monitoring systems, while Veekmas market an underground motor grader to maintain road surfaces and reduce tyre wear. Major mining companies are also aware of the benefits from managing their internal mineral extraction support sector more effectively. Preston Chiaro, Group Executive, Technology and Innovation, Rio Tinto, presented at the company’s Investor Seminar on 09 Oct 2012. He emphasised that Rio Tinto would: - focus on optimising operating assets to achieve industry leading performance. - standardise global asset management processes to drive down costs. - adopt a systematic approach to innovation to maximise the value derived. Whether through internal teams, such as those in Rio Tinto, or through the wider mineral extraction support service sector, CRU believes that this sector will be the incubator for a new wave of change & innovation affecting the enti

re mining industry. The mining boom is not over for those in this sector that embrace and create this change. They will continue to flourish. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 8 of 13 December 2012 Copper Studies www.crugroup.com ### No change in the smelting and refining sector While some have fretted over the future of the commodity boom, those in other sectors have a very different story to tell. CRU believes there never was a boom for copper smelters and refiners. Moving along the value chain, copper smelters and refineries have struggled in the current boom: - There has been little capacity rationalisation despite a persistent concentrate shortage. - China has continued to invest in capacity to become ‘self sufficient’. - Raw material cost inflation has been rife, while TC/RCs have fallen. - There has also been a general increase in the cost of scrap material and a general transfer in the value of scrap from copper smelters and refiners to scrap owners. The two charts below reinforce the point. The chart on the left shows how the smelter share of the LME copper price in percentage terms has fallen over the last decade. The chart on the right shows how the value has also fallen in absolute terms. Smelters have lost out in relative... ...and absolute terms in the boom

On the one hand, Chinese overcapacity in smelting has created a seller’s market for concentrate suppliers, who have been able to reduce TC/RCs and remove other favourable terms over the last decade. Some in China would argue, however, that the loss made in the smelting sector is a small price to pay if it lowers the overall copper price paid for all Chinese imported material. What is clear is that China’s appetite to build more copper smelting and refining capacity in the future has not been materially impacted by this dismal sector performance. Nearly 5Mt of new smelting capacity is expected to be constructed over the next five years and as a result global utilisation rates will remain stubbornly below 74%. One positive for smelters is that CRU expects annual contract TC/RCs to rise almost every year out to 2017. However, the principal drivers of this increase; a reduction in the value of by-products and © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 9 of 13 Copper Studies December 2012 www.crugroup.com declining concentrate quality, means these increases simply track a similar increase in the smelter breakeven price. Overall, the copper smelting sector has not experienced a commodity boom and will continue to struggle until the amount of idled capacity begins to fall. Smelter margins will not improve from 2012 to 2017 and therefore there will be no copp

er commodity boom for this sector going forward. ### For the semis industry, a warning of things to come? China’s dominant position in primary aluminium smelting is a well reported fact. Like copper smelting, some Chinese players believe this dominance has put downward pressure on margins to be made in that part of the value chain. China has built on this position of strength and is also now investing heavily in aluminium semis capacity. The chart below shows Chinese aluminium rolling capacity. CRU predicts that mill utilisation rates will fall by 30% between 2011 and 2015 as mill capacity doubles. Export markets for high value products such as aerospace, lidstock & autobody sheet remain difficult for China to penetrate today but there is plenty of potential for a low value product export boom. This situation shown in the chart is simply not sustainable. China is currently absorbing the idled capacity but what is the long term future of this semis capacity? What impact will this have on China and the global market? CRU fears that this will not remain a China contained issue and that the global aluminium semis industry will experience even greater competitive threats from China in the future. #### Some in the aluminium semis sector think the boom will continue 20000 100%

The Chinese copper semis industry does not yet have the advantage of a low raw material cost base like the aluminium industry. However, as it begins to dominate copper smelting this will come. Concerns are already being raised with excess capacity reported in sectors such as copper wirerod. Like aluminium, what China does with this surplus capacity is the key question to answer if you want to predict the profitability of the global semis industry going forward. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 10 of 13 December 2012 Copper Studies www.crugroup.com ### Commodity investors will have to work harder If you are going to “buy” a commodity, then it follows that you expect the price to rise. Since 2004, there has been a simple commodity story in place to explain this expectation and it had two chapters to it. - The first is the expectation that the US dollar will be weaker over time because the US will, in relative terms, become less important. Thus, if you sell US dollars to purchase a dollar-denominated commodity, as the USD becomes weaker; your commodity becomes more valuable. - The second chapter in the commodity story is Development Economics 101. As countries become more industrialized, they use more metal. As people move from the country to the city more infrastructure is required. Consumers get wealthier and purchase m

ore goods. Eventually countries start to produce, and even export, higher value products. During the last decade, the surge in Chinese development related demand has outpaced existing supply plans. Going forward there are several populous economies (India, Indonesia) that could act as a catalyst like this in the future. A belief in these two facts, combined with a simple strategy of broad exposure to commodity markets, was enough to propel investment volumes, support commodity prices and create enviable returns for investors. The support for commodity prices can be seen in the chart below. CRU regularly analyses the Comex copper price against the CFTC net position data for Managed Money traders. By undertaking this analysis, it is very clear that the sustained upward move in the copper price from a low of $2,760/t in December 2008 to $10,070/t in February 2011 would have been impossible without investor buying in copper. #### There is a clear relationship between investor activity and price. The breakneck growth in China is a thing of the past. High metals prices have done their job, there is new capacity coming on stream and the commodity markets look adequately supplied, for now. Given all the market uncertainty investors also need to be comfortable with volatility. © 2012 CRU International Limited **confidential** Page 11 of 13 Copper Studies December 2012 www.crugroup.com Those commodity investors that are comfortable in volatile markets are preparing to take advantage of forthcoming price highs and lows. The boom for some commodity investors is over. All will have to work harder to succeed in this sector. Consequently, dumb, broad commodity or commodity equity investment is unlikely to be as successful as it was in the past. However sophisticated investors able to identify individual commodities (such as palladium, tin, zinc & uranium) or low cost asset developers can continue to make superior returns. ### Conclusion So in conclusion, is the commodity boom over for copper? 2011 looks to have been the peak year for copper prices in the current copper cycle. However, the market will still deliver the necessary growth drivers to continu

e the boom, by pre-2006 standards: - Refined metal consumption prospects look relatively strong going forward, with growth in excess of 4% per annum expected through to 2017. - Strong mine supply, if delivered, will however create market surpluses until at least 2017. - Prices will retreat from 2015 but remain far higher than industry norms. As previously discussed, positive profit expectations are a pre-requisite of any prolonged commodity boom. Volume growth and price growth without profit is not a boom scenario. Here the picture is more mixed and only certain parts of the copper value chain will experience supernormal profits going forward: - Mining margins for low cost producers also peaked in 2011. They have fallen in 2012 and will retreat again from 2015. But throughout the entire 2012-2017 period margins will remain high, by historical standards. The boom is not over for low cost copper miners yet. - The boom is probably over for high cost miners and developers. They face a multitude of competitive threats, creating a squeeze on their production base. However, shareholders and owners #### In conclusion, the commodity boom… Low cost

All miners will be seeking advice from this sector to maintain margins in the face of falling revenues. Those that deliver truly innovative ways of doing this will flourish. - There has been and will be no boom for copper smelters and refineries. They continue to face tough times, despite a likely improvement in headline TC/RCs. China will continue to build copper smelting capacity, depressing utilisation rates. TC/RCs are only forecast to improve as by-product revenues fall and concentrate qualities deteriorate. Margins in this sector will remain low. - The semis industry prospects will be determined by the actions of the Chinese semis industry. In copper, the domestic industry lacks the cost advantage seen in aluminium, which will be required in order to become a large scale exporter. If that were to change, China could utilise surplus copper semis capacity to launch bigger export drives. - Investors are not leaving t

he commodity sector and copper remains an attractive asset.  However, the commodity boom for market investors is over and they will have to work far harder to make returns in this sector.  Only sophisticated investors able to identify individual commodities (such as palladium, tin, zinc & uranium) or low cost asset developers can continue to make superior returns. 

Indeed, if we were forced to try and summarise our outlook in one sentence, it would probably build on the last bullet point.  CRU believes that the Commodity Boom continues but that you will have to work harder in the future to capture its benefits.
